--- court opens ---
[00:04] JUDGE: All right, good morning everyone. The The next case is the Board of Trustees of the University of South Florida versus USF Financing Corporation at all. Ms. Sandridge?

--- appellant's argument ---
[00:18] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: If it may please the court, my name is Hala Sandridge. I represent the University of South Florida Board of Trustees, and I would like to reserve 5 minutes for rebuttal.
[00:25] JUDGE: Yes, ma'am.
[00:26] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: So, I'd like to address the jurisdictional issue first. Um Judge Labrit, last time
[00:31] JUDGE: déjà vu all over again.
[00:33] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: You had questioned whether these type of interlocutory appeals should be brought now or at the end of the case. And I took away from your comments that you agree that the court technically has jurisdiction based upon the motion that was filed and the wording of rule 9.130. But what I heard from you was perhaps a prudential concern. Um which is how many appeals can a party um raise a sovereign immunity defense when it loses and then it appeals. Is Is that a fair statement, Your Honor?
[01:07] JUDGE: It's been a while since we had that conversation, so I'll accept the way you've described it with a with a qualified acceptance. I I'm I have a question for you that I think in this instance narrows it down. Here at least we don't have the judge saying, "I didn't rule on sovereign immunity grounds."
[01:24] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: That's correct.
[01:24] JUDGE: And
[01:27] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: So, let me make sure I understand what we have here. We have count four on the Mersa, which is a direct contract with USF, which is a waiver of sovereign immunity.
[01:38] JUDGE: That's correct.
[01:39] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: And your argument below and here, I think, is that the measure of damages that they're claiming for count four and perhaps to some extent, I'm not sure about this and I need clarity, the remaining counts, which I think are more or less quasi-contract type claims that are not again direct against USF on the basis of a written contract. But I had trouble deciphering in your brief if you were limiting your damages you're arguing if I understand it correctly that the damages are precluded under principles of sovereign immunity the damages claims that they've made are precluded under principles of sovereign immunity. Do I have it right so far?
[02:25] JUDGE: Somewhat.
[02:26] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Okay. At least with respect to MERCE I understand the argument. I'm not sure I agree with it, but I understand what you're doing. I would like to know if you're making the same arguments today as to counts um I think it's three two three and six which are still alive and to which I can't tell if you've attacked on sovereign immunity grounds. What's going on there?
[02:52] JUDGE: Yeah, these are great questions and I have answers for you.
[02:55] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Good.
[02:56] JUDGE: So so IUP has a count against USF for breach of the direct entry agreement. That's the only
[03:06] JUDGE: Is that the MERCE?
[03:07] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Um
[03:08] JUDGE: The direct entry agreement?
[03:10] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: think it
[03:11] JUDGE: It Everybody calls these things different things. It's hard to keep track.
[03:13] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: the direct entry program and um the the point of that contract is that IUP entered into an agreement with USF to directly recruit students who were admissible to USF. That's one program. And and that is between IUP and USF.
[03:34] JUDGE: And that's count four?
[03:35] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: I'm sorry.
[03:35] JUDGE: Is that count four?
[03:37] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: That is Yes, I I guess I would call it count four. Yes, it is it is their
[03:42] JUDGE: And that's the And that's the only agreement that USF is a signatory to.
[03:47] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: With IUP.
[03:49] JUDGE: And and it it also gets called the MERCE. Help me out here cuz
[03:53] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: I I don't call I don't know if it's the MERCE They called it the MERCE. They called it the prime agreement in their brief, which I don't know where that came from.
[04:01] JUDGE: be helpful. If you get when you guys come back, come up with a universal
[04:05] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: It We have always called it that. We have always called it the direct entry agreement because it allows students to directly enter USF. Then there is this other program that's a completely different program. And it is a program where the parties entered into a complicated complicated transaction to set up an entity where the financing corporation was a party, a stockholder, and IUP's subsidiary was a stockholder. And it ran a program to bring in students. These are all international students who are not directly admissible into USF. Completely separate program. And that's why this is important, Your Honor. Because this is not about the amount of damages. It's about this claim for damages that are based upon terms of contracts that USF did not sign.
[05:04] JUDGE: I appreciate you focusing on this cuz I thought about it when we were getting here. And I looked at what the contract says. I think it's the one we're talking about, the MERCE, the direct entry agreement.
[05:13] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Mhm.
[05:13] JUDGE: The one that USF has waived sovereign immunity on, right?
[05:16] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Correct.
[05:17] JUDGE: And what it said about compensation We talked a little bit about compensation last time, maybe when we were in Arcadia. But this time I looked at this and thought, you know, what is there a limitation, a specific limitation or quantification in the compensation provision? What I think it says is that USF will pay per the schedule.
[05:39] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Mhm.
[05:40] JUDGE: And then in the last sentence of that paragraph, it says, "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, the parties agree that IUP maintains all rights to any and all claims under applicable laws against USF for breach and non-payment of such compensation payments. Is it your position that that limits that that's a strict limitation to the schedule payments?
[06:04] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: No. No, your honor. Again,
[06:05] JUDGE: What limitations are there?
[06:08] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: is we owe them under this contract for recruiting international students. That that's what that provision is for. We agreed to pay them for recruiting international students. When we terminated that agreement, we have agreed and we have not moved for summary judgment on this count. We have agreed that if we wrongfully terminated the direct entry agreement, and I I would ask you to turn to page seven of my brief with the chart. I know there's been some questions about the charts, but I really think it helps you understand that this is a separate contract, a separate transaction. So that when we terminated it, we have agreed if we wrongfully terminated it and they can prove damages, lost profits from our termination, they're entitled to those damages. Now, if I could take you to the other part of the chart, where there is this other transaction with other parties with agreements that USF did not sign with IUP. That's where they're claiming these damages.
[07:09] JUDGE: And so what when have you challenged those counts on sovereign immunity?
[07:13] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: It's not It's not a separate count. That's the That is exactly, your honor, the problem here and you're actually hitting the nail on the head. That's what they're doing here. They're trying in their count that they have for breach of the direct entry agreement to claim these damages
[07:29] JUDGE: So
[07:30] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: under other contracts.
[07:31] JUDGE: we're at the point where your your friend on the other side, I think, aptly characterized this as effectively a ruling on a motion in limine having to do with the damages that are available for the claims that seem to morph between the counts, but anyway, tell me why
[07:52] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: I don't see that, Your Honor. Here is Here is why. Here is why. So, let me give you the Mirelli case. All right? The Mirelli case is a case out of the Florida Supreme Court, affirmed by Rojas. In Mirelli, it enters into an agreement to build or renovate a stadium for the County of Brevard. The County of Brevard says, "Um we want you to do this extra work." They did it. They didn't sign a contract. There were no change orders. They did the work. And the Supreme Court said, "Look, you have to have a written agreement with express provisions for that work."
[08:28] JUDGE: But this isn't extra work. This is breach of an express written agreement for which there are consequential damages. And some of the consequential damages happen to do with They're not losses based on these other contracts.
[08:41] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: consequential damages. That's what That's how they're trying to get around sovereign immunity. It's to say that they are a consequence of the breach of this agreement. They're not. They're a consequence of the termination of the Pathways program, which was a program we did not have with IUP.
[08:57] JUDGE: Wasn't that a question of fact whether it's reasonably foreseeable? Doesn't Doesn't that all go together and and defeat a claim for summary judgment?
[09:06] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: It doesn't, Your Honor. Again, it can be decided as a matter of law. It is a matter of contract interpretation. The contracts say what they say. These are two separate two separate programs entirely. You can't take the damages that their co-plaintiffs lost on. These are claims that their co-plaintiffs lost. And say, "Okay, now we're going to claim that as damages because you can't sue any longer to get your damages under the Pathways program, and we're going to bring them in as consequential damages under a contract over which we had no right to even claim those damages. If it as a matter of law, that's not only foreseeable, it's just not even consequential damages and I would say your honor that one of their major arguments in this that they said in their answer brief is that this was a partnership. This was not a partnership with USF. As you folks know USF cannot enter into a partnership and so it was structured in a way so that USF could not be responsible for anything under the pathway program with IUP. It had no contract with IUP. It only had a contract for this direct entry program. So to try and back door in these terms into a program of which it's not related, it's not consequential damages, your honor. We've cited the cases. Consequential damages flow from the breach of the agreement. Those damages don't flow from the breach of the direct entry agreement. The direct entry agreement when we terminated that just said they don't get to get commissions anymore for the students that they directly recruit. Lost profits is completely different and so if damages flowed from that, which is what all these damages they're seeking are. So whether it is the shared services, whether it is the administration, the marketing, all of it for the pathways program, has nothing to do and doesn't flow from the breach of our direct entry contract. So they're not foreseeable. I would also argue that as a matter of law if a if the sovereign enters into a contract specifically for amounts and it knows that sovereign immunity protects them to just the terms of that contract that it would not be foreseeable as a matter of law for someone to come in and argue that you should have known you were going to be responsible for any damages flowing from the Pathways program when they were absolutely sheltered from IUP being able to claim damages under the Pathways program. So, for those reasons we believe that it is absolutely a an issue of law that can be decided and should have been decided on summary judgment. Um, going back then to the jurisdictional issue, Your Honor. I think what I'm trying to say here is that we did have a very valid basis for our sovereign immunity argument and that, you know, when when a party is claiming $24 million against effectively the state of Florida, the university, which is an agency, sovereign immunity is meant to deal with that early and directly. Um, as you know, sovereign immunity not only protects a lawsuit, but it protects the treasury of the state. And so, we do feel it is appropriate under these circumstances.
[13:06] JUDGE: What's your best case for the proposition that they're not immune from liability, but you can start carving out certain categories of loss?
[13:16] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Um, and again it it it's not the categories of loss that's the issue here. It's what term supports that category of loss. So, Your Honor, um an example. They sued us for shared services, $2.6 million for shared services. And by the way, I would say we're entitled to a reversal on just that issue because they don't even respond in the brief to that issue. But, nevertheless, shared services doesn't come from any term of contract that IUP and USF signed. That is There is no contractual term, an express contractual term for these amounts. And therefore, under Miarelli, which I think is one of our best cases, if there is no is no express term in the contract, you don't get to avoid it by saying it's consequential damages. So, consequential damages, I think, we come at it two different ways. Number one, does it flow from the breach? And here it the the these amounts that they're claiming don't don't flow from the breach. But, more importantly, I think the issue this court has to decide today is whether consequential damages can trump sovereign immunity when a transaction was specifically designed to limit the liability of the sovereign based upon constitutional principles.
[14:48] JUDGE: Well, and and that's why I asked you about the provision in the agreement that seems pretty open-ended where IUP reserved all rights to any and all claims under applicable laws for breach and non-payment of compensation payments.
[15:03] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: It
[15:04] JUDGE: And what I hear you telling us is a whole bunch of legal arguments about why the damages are not consequential to the breach because we're dealing with the sovereign, but this is what the sovereign wrote in their agreement and it's broad.
[15:22] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Mhm. So, sovereign immunity principles still apply. So, so do consequential damage principles. I I don't disagree that Let me give you an example. Let Let me give you an example. If If you could say that because we terminated the direct entry agreement, that these were consequential damages, then they would have an argument. But But they are not consequential damages of the breach of the direct entry agreement. They are damages that they're claiming that were owed to their subsidiary or owed to the company, and their subsidiary and their company lost on those claims. So, now they're going to try and bootstrap them on their claim under the direct entry agreement. So, So, yes, Your Honor, normal principles would apply, but here they're not even consequential damages. They are just a way of trying to get around sovereign immunity. That That is why they have categorized this characterized this as consequential damages is because they are trying to get around the fact that there are no contract terms. And that is, I think, the interplay between sovereign immunity and consequential damages that that this court is facing today.
[16:44] JUDGE: You're right at your 5 minutes. If you'd like to save some time.
[16:47] APPELLANT'S COUNSEL: Thank you.
[16:47] JUDGE: Yes.

--- appellee's argument ---
[17:02] APPELLEE'S COUNSEL: Good morning, and may it please the court. My name is Sam Salario, and I'm here for Appellee in two. I I think I just heard my colleague on the other side say, as in support of the sovereign immunity argument, that these contracts were specifically designed to limit USF's liability. What people do when they want to limit their liability for consequential damages is they put a consequential damages waiver or limitation in their contract. You probably signed plenty of those contracts for any service you receive at your home, for any third party you hired to come do work at your house. Courts see them every day of the week. USF is asking this court to insert into a contract a consequential damages waiver that it did not negotiate for. The most straightforward path to affirmance is to or to to decision is to recognize that and affirm under Rojas and United Capital. One of the most arresting facts in this case is pretty buried in USF's briefs, but below USF conceded both that it breached an express written contract and that it caused into's damages. The appendix at 10:37 has Miss Sandridge telling the trial court, quote, "For summary judgment, we're assuming a breach and we're assuming a causal connection." And on the same page, again, quote, "We are accepting for the purpose of this argument that there was a breach and there was a causal chain." This was not Judge Labrit concessional adjacent concession adjacent. We are squarely in concession territory and if you read that page of the record, it's not qualified. The only issue that survives that concession is whether the consequential damages concededly caused by USF's conceded breach of the contract were reasonably foreseeable. That's a classic fact question for trial. USF says it's a question of sovereign immunity, but that's wrong. It is my run contract interpretation and enforcement. The a breaching party is liable for damages even though they don't arise directly under the contract that it could have reasonably anticipated at the time of contracting. And I think you hear that actually in in my colleague's argument, right? She keeps using phrases like not foreseeable as a matter of law, not real consequential damages. Those aren't sovereign immunity arguments. Those are arguments about whether they should have gotten a summary judgment on causation or foreseeability. And you know, that's not within the scope of this court's review on appeal from an order denying a motion that asserts an entitlement to sovereign immunity. Rojas tells the court that questions about how to interpret a contract are contract law questions, not immunity questions. United Capital tells the court that questions about how to remedy the breach of a state contract are contract law questions, not immunity questions. But flouting both precedents and evading its own concessions, USF relabels the classic contract law foreseeability as sovereign immunity. Rojas and United Capital prohibit that. USF is bound by the same contract law rules as everyone else. So having agreed to the what I'll call the direct admit marketing agreement uh with the legislature's blessing, USF does not enjoy a special privilege to demand a summary judgment on damages no other contract party could ask for. Nor does it have a special privilege to take a non-final appeal on damages that no other contract party could take. Judge Labrit, you you stole my line. I was about to say this is deja vu all over again, and it is. We were here last month arguing another piecemeal appeal in which USF camouflage a contract interpretation question as a sovereign immunity question. Five days after OA and OA in which by the way the parties and the panel discussed extensively and at length how the same principles we're talking about today doomed that appeal. USF dismissed its appeal. It's unclear why USF thinks it's a good idea to resurrect the same arguments with a different panel, but the court should not permit a let's see how argument goes strategy here. Regardless of what USF does after this argument, this court should affirm on the merits because USF's summary judgment motion never raised a legitimate sovereign immunity question to begin with. I think I just want to go to kind of the essence of what I think this blurring of the lines between what's really an argument about what's legit consequential damages and what's sovereign immunity. I think that USF's appeal really hinges on a single sentence in its initial brief. And that sentence and the principle it kind of tries to smuggle in gets things exactly backwards. USF's appeal works only if this court accepts a hidden default rule that I don't think USF wants to say expressly that the state by signing a contract agrees only to those damages the contract specifically itemizes and is the state has somehow opted out of every other foreseeable consequence of a breach. That premise is wrong. The default rule of contract law, every contract state or private, is that a breach gives rise to the non parties non breaching parties right to recover all reasonably foreseeable consequential damages. Parties who want to limit that default rule negotiate a consequential damages waiver. USF didn't negotiate for one here and the directed mint marketing agreement doesn't have one. So at the So USF agreed at the time of contracting that all reasonably foreseeable consequential damages are recoverable. As applied here, that default rule includes the consequential damages flow that that were in the contracts that USF was a part of. This was a group of of linked or similar contracts executed on the same day as part of the same essential transaction and I I think you just heard it from Miss Sandridge in in her opening presentation that were done that way because of constitutional concerns around a state entity being a shareholder uh in a for-profit enterprise.
[24:08] JUDGE: And that that's where the chart comes in in determining the reasonable foreseeability, correct? That it comes in at that point, not at the point in determining sovereign immunity.
[24:19] APPELLEE'S COUNSEL: Right. And And I think to add on to that, right? I think it just illustrates that at the time of contracting, USF knew what these other contracts were and knew how the termination of the directed mint marketing agreement might affect them. Um But But USF's appeal lives or dies on one sentence that smuggles in the opposite rule. At page 15 of its brief, USF tells the court, quote, "But foreseeable damages could only relate to damages under the direct entry agreement, the only agreement USF signed in which I in which IUP alleged USF breached." That one sentence is the only place where USF kind of asserts the rule that it needs to win, and take it away, and all you're left with are fact disputes about foreseeability. Two things about that sentence. First, it isn't a sovereign immunity argument at all. It's a contract law argument about the scope of foreseeable damages based on a breach of an express written contract. That's the tell. USF's appeal is at bottom contract law foreseeability dressed in sovereign immunity clothing. That alone is reason to affirm. The second interesting thing about that sentence is it carries no citation behind it. None. That's because no Florida court that I can tell has held that foreseeable damage damages from a breach of an express state contract can only relate to amounts the contract itemizes. The reason for the absence of that law And and by the way, just to talk about the best case Mirelli, Mirelli wasn't a case of damages that weren't expressly stated in the contract or provided for. Mirelli was a case of imposing obligations on the state that weren't included in the state's contract. It was a contractor who performed out of contract work without a change order, and the holding there is you can't be liable on the contract for work that's not included in the contract, not that damages are somehow limited. Foreseeable consequential damages by definition arise from from relationship or from losses the non-breaching party incurs in its dealings, which are often with third parties, that could have been reasonably anticipated at contracting. They come from outside the contract's payment schedule. If they were limited to things that were inside the contract, there'd be no need to call them consequential damages. We'd just call them direct damages. Um USF's rule would basically write consequential damages out of state contracts entirely because I think in USF's telling the state can't reasonably foresee anything that's not included in the contract. Foreseeability is not a stretch on this record. The four contracts were signed the same day, drafted as as part of part of a single deal, and were linked together as a cohesive whole. So, USF knew when it signed that its breach of the direct admit marketing agreement is going to have consequences for these other contracts, not a damages theory we invented. Um so, when USF tells the court that foreseeable damages could only relate to amounts the direct admit marketing agreement itemizes, USF is asking for two things at once. A consequential damages waiver it didn't negotiate for, and a rule of contract law that no court has ever announced. The state doesn't get special rules of contract interpretation and enforcement. Rohas and United Capital are clear about that. And the state doesn't get a damages limitation it never bargained for. And unless the panel has any questions for me, I think that covers it. So, I'm happy to field anything.
[28:21] JUDGE: Thank you, sir. You have your full 5 minutes if you choose to use it.
[28:32] APPELLEE'S COUNSEL: Yes, thank you, Your Honor. So, I'd like to go back to this idea that these are consequential damages. And let me be clear. What USF's position is is that these claims are not based on terms in any contract with USF and therefore are barred by sovereign immunity. And that the only way they get around that is by arguing consequential damages. So, first we have to decide whether or not these terms exist in any contract with USF. And I I I think what I hear is a concession that there is no contract with USF that says we're responsible for shared services. We're responsible for administrative amounts. We're responsible for anything under the stockholder agreement. So, we can put that aside. There is no such agreement with those terms. Sovereign immunity applies. Their only way of getting around that fact is to say, "Well, you're responsible because our damages under those contracts flow from your breach of direct entry." That is an impossibility and let me explain why. Going back to the chart, um in the chart you will see that there is one program here for direct entry between USF and IUP. Let's assume that this scenario played out. USF terminated the direct entry agreement, didn't want IUP recruiting international international students directly, and kept the pathways program. Right? And the pathways program just ran. There is no damages that IUP suffered related to the pathways program, which kept going because our termination of the direct entry agreement only stopped their payments under the direct entry agreement. Now, let's assume the opposite. That we didn't terminate the direct entry agreement, and we just terminated the pathways agreement with the company. There are no [snorts] damages, no harm to IUP under our contract with it because it kept going. We were doing exactly what we agreed to do, which was to pay them for recruiting international students directly admissible. There is no way that our termination of the direct entry agreement causes them any damages under the pathways program because they're two separate programs. They are signed on the same day and that is the only connection. That they are signed on the same day, but no damages flow directly from the termination of the direct entry agreement by our termination of the pathways agreement. They flow to the parties that were part of the agreement with USF to run the pathways program, but not IUP. If if I will admit if I can't get you there to agree with me on that, then I can't win this appeal. And that is the issue that I need this court to address today. And I do think that is an issue that is a matter of law. I argued it below as a matter of law, and I'm arguing it again as a matter of law. And I think that that issue if you can agree with me on that issue, that that is not a consequential damages, then we default back to okay, so where are the terms in the contract with USF? And they're not, and sovereign immunity applies. Thank you.

--- court closes ---
[32:15] JUDGE: Thank you, counsel. Well done. The next case is the case of Larry Silaway as personal rep of Larry James Silaway versus Brandon Crossroads Mall.

transcript_sufficient.instructions: Does `transcript` contain enough of an appellate oral argument — questions from judges and answers from counsel about the merits — to judge how the bench is responding? Answer false if it is mostly ceremony, announcements, silence markers, or garbled text.

is_oral_argument.instructions: Is `transcript` an oral argument in an appeal, as opposed to a ceremony, induction, speech, or announcement?

bench_skepticism_toward_appellant.instructions: How does the bench treat the APPELLANT's position in `transcript`? Judge the judges' words to and about the appellant's argument, not the strength of the argument itself.
criteria: Receptive: the bench's questions to this side are clarifying or friendly, and judges signal agreement or help counsel develop the argument.
Mildly probing: ordinary testing questions with no sign the bench doubts the position.
Skeptical: judges push back on the position, raise contrary authority or facts, or ask counsel to justify it.
Strongly skeptical: judges reject the position's premises or express doubt it can succeed.
Hostile: judges are dismissive or exasperated, openly say the position fails, or admonish counsel.

bench_skepticism_toward_appellee.instructions: How does the bench treat the APPELLEE's position in `transcript`? Judge the judges' words to and about the appellee's argument, not the strength of the argument itself.
criteria: Receptive: the bench's questions to this side are clarifying or friendly, and judges signal agreement or help counsel develop the argument.
Mildly probing: ordinary testing questions with no sign the bench doubts the position.
Skeptical: judges push back on the position, raise contrary authority or facts, or ask counsel to justify it.
Strongly skeptical: judges reject the position's premises or express doubt it can succeed.
Hostile: judges are dismissive or exasperated, openly say the position fails, or admonish counsel.

ruling_lean.instructions: From the judges' questions and comments in `transcript` alone, which way does the bench appear to lean?

criteria.affirm: The bench appears inclined to affirm the lower court's ruling.
criteria.reverse: The bench appears inclined to reverse or vacate the lower court's ruling, in whole or in part.
criteria.mixed_or_unclear: The bench gives no clear signal, or different judges signal different directions.

panel_disagreement.instructions: Do the judges signal disagreement with one another in `transcript` — one judge pushing back on, correcting, or distancing themself from another judge's point?

bench_says_issue_unraised.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` say that an issue was not raised, briefed, or preserved by a party?

bench_raises_jurisdiction.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` question whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the appeal or whether the order is appealable?

bench_says_appellant_counsel_not_answeri.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` express frustration or impatience that the APPELLANT's counsel is not answering the question that was asked? Ordinary follow-up questions do not count.

bench_says_appellee_counsel_not_answerin.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` express frustration or impatience that the APPELLEE's counsel is not answering the question that was asked? Ordinary follow-up questions do not count.

appellant_concedes_point.instructions: Does the APPELLANT's counsel in `transcript` concede a point that weakens the appellant's own position? Agreeing with a judge who is helping their side does not count.

appellee_concedes_point.instructions: Does the APPELLEE's counsel in `transcript` concede a point that weakens the appellee's own position? Agreeing with a judge who is helping their side does not count.

bench_remarks_on_pro_se_status.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` comment on a party being self-represented (pro se), for example noting that a party has no lawyer?

bench_remarks_on_pro_se_filing_quality.instructions: Does a judge in `transcript` comment on the quality, clarity, or adequacy of a self-represented party's filings or arguments?

bench_posture_toward_trial_court.instructions: How does the bench characterize the trial court's handling of the case in `transcript`?

criteria.deferential: Judges defend or excuse the trial court's decision, or emphasize its discretion.
criteria.neutral: Judges discuss the trial court's decision without evaluating it.
criteria.critical: Judges criticize the trial court's reasoning, process, or findings.
criteria.not_discussed: The trial court's handling is not discussed.

legend.4: Hostile: judges are dismissive or exasperated, openly say the position fails, or admonish counsel.
